extracted.intended_audience: NIH extramural investigators, biomedical PIs, grant applicants and research administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Practical commentary and explanatory guidance about NIH extramural grant policies, review practices, and submission strategy — aimed at biomedical investigators navigating application, review, and award processes. Covers procedural notices, reviewer behavior, paylines/success rates, and study section organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of scope (NOT-OD-26-007 definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change in the direction, aims, objectives, purposes, or type of research training, identified in the approved project. This can include changes to Aims, Objectives, Titles, and Abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in scope become new terms and conditions of award, with which recipients must comply. The notice explicitly states that changes renegotiated to align with agency priorities are included. The blog emphasizes that even a change of Title qualifies as a change of scope and therefore alters award T&Cs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of Title treated as change of scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A change in the Title is a change of scope which becomes new terms and conditions of award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even seemingly cosmetic edits to titles or abstracts can be enforced as new conditions; PIs should treat requests to alter titles/abstracts as potentially limiting the permitted research directions and consult Program/awards management if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior contact/LOI requirement for large budgets (historical requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants requesting $500,000 or more in direct costs in any one budget period were previously required to contact the funding Institute or Center (IC) before application submission and include a cover letter identifying the Program Official contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prior requirement functioned as a gatekeeping mechanism (ICs could reject or decline assignment). The blog notes NIH removed this requirement (effective immediately at time of writing) to reduce applicant burden and to reduce Program staff gatekeeping power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program Officer gatekeeping role
rubrics_metrics.description: Program Officers historically could approve/deny LOIs, disallow conference-support applications, limit large-budget R01s, and otherwise act as gatekeepers before peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gatekeeping can be harmful (arbitrary blocking) but also protective (preventing clearly inappropriate awards). Removal of gatekeeping (e.g., LOI removal) reduces informal PO control but shifts risk that problematic proposals might proceed; PIs should be aware of changing informal PO advice and its consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on spending on unapproved vertebrate animal species
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot spend grant funds on research using a vertebrate animal species not mentioned in the original proposal unless you complete paperwork with OLAW and request a change from your Program Officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as an example of a clear black-and-white compliance rule even in otherwise flexible areas; PIs must follow required extramural compliance steps before changing species used under an award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to Previous Review (resubmission evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For revised applications (resubmissions), reviewers historically had a header to assess 'Response to Previous Review' — evaluating the quality of the applicant's responses to prior criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog notes this box was prominent historically but later de-emphasized; reviewers are nevertheless expected to evaluate how well the resubmission addressed prior concerns. PIs should clearly and directly document responses to prior review criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Comments to Applicant should not determine overall impact score
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH inserted an 'Additional Comments to Applicant' box which was intended to be a pressure-relief valve and reviewers were told these comments 'should not be considered in providing an overall impact/priority score.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although guidance exists, the blog cautions reviewers' informal commentary often functions as justification for scoring and may leak into scoring decisions; applicants should still take these comments seriously but understand they are not supposed to count toward the overall impact score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid benchmarking resubmissions to prior scores (reviewer instruction vs practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are instructed to review revised grants 'without reference to how the prior version scored' and not to benchmark to prior scores, but in practice benchmarking often occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIs should both address prior criticisms thoroughly and be aware that reviewers may (explicitly or implicitly) punish or compare to prior versions. The blog highlights the tension between policy and reviewer behavior, and the potential for resubmissions to score worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission limits and A1/A2 policy history
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH used to allow up to A2 amended versions; later policy reduced the allowable resubmissions (e.g., limit to A1) and attempted to ban resubmitting essentially the same proposal as a new application (with subsequent backdown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy history affects strategy: how many times you can revise before having to submit as new. Track current agency rules for allowed resubmissions when planning revision strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: CSR triage / Discussed vs Not Discussed rates (procedural metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR instituted enhanced triage procedures increasing the proportion of proposals that are Not Discussed (ND) — the blog cites ~70% ND vs prior ~50%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher triage rates mean more proposals (including revised ones) may not be discussed; applicants should be strategic about resubmission timing and manage expectations about discussion likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit payline by percentile (funding probability metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding decisions follow an implicit payline represented by percentile score: the percentile at which proposals, and anything better, are likely to be funded (e.g., ~4%ile in FY2025 vs higher in prior years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NIH Report 302 and RePORT analytics to estimate payline and the funding probability at your percentile; changes year-to-year can strongly affect funding chances and submission strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding Rate (per-PI) vs Success Rate (per-application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding Rate measures whether a PI who applied in a fiscal year received an award (per-PI), whereas Success Rate is per-application (per submission). These are distinct metrics and can give different impressions of difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIs should understand which metric is being quoted and use the appropriate one when assessing competitiveness (e.g., Funding Rate can understate per-application difficulty if PIs submit many applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Study section composition / IC capture influences review outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The background and dominant representation on a study section (e.g., an 'NIAAA-dominated' panel) will influence relative scoring of topic-specific proposals; panels dominated by members from a particular IC tend to favor that IC's topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment to a generalist vs IC-specific panel can advantage or disadvantage certain topics; PIs should consider assignment preferences and the implications of CSR consolidation that groups applications by science rather than IC.

rubrics_metrics.name: ENQUIRE evaluation criteria for study sections
rubrics_metrics.description: ENQUIRE integrates data and stakeholder input to determine whether changes in study section focus/scope are needed to 'facilitate the identification of high impact science, with special consideration of emerging science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ENQUIRE assessments can lead to closing, continuing, or creating study sections; PIs should watch ENQUIRE outcomes as study section realignment affects review culture and funding patterns for specific topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of special HIV/AIDS due dates (procedural deadline change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-standard application dates for HIV/AIDS grant proposals (historic special due dates) were eliminated, consolidating them into standard NIH cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affects submission timing strategy for investigators who previously used additional HIV/AIDS deadlines to space submissions; PIs should plan around the standard NIH calendar going forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic analysis as a metric for grant terminations
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical analyses (Fielding-Miller et al., Lancet) assessed demographics of PIs with terminated grants (e.g., higher termination rates for women, Hispanic/Latino, Black/African American, American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander compared with 2024 NIH-funded PI demographics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog highlights that demographic disparities are measurable outcomes and can be used as a data-based account of policy effects; such metrics inform advocacy and legal/policy responses but are not a grant-production checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantaged socio-economic background (former NIH diversity criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents were asked whether they qualified under the NIH's former 'section c.' disadvantaged socio-economic background criteria; grants with investigators who had disadvantaged backgrounds were reported as 2.54 times more likely to be terminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical NIH diversity/eligibility criteria can surface in data analyses of funding and termination patterns. PIs who used such designations in applications should be aware of how those designations are handled in policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word/phrase removal requests (titles/abstracts) as de facto content control
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses (word cloud) and anecdotal reports show commonly removed words include 'equity', 'diverse', 'disparate', 'racial', 'gender' — Program staff are reportedly requesting these changes prior to issuing Notices of Award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog cautions that being asked to 'just change words' may be instructive: removing certain framing may constrain the angles from which a PI can pursue their research. PIs should weigh the risk of acceding to such requests versus the potential of losing funding or changing scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-year funding effects on paylines and new awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-year funding commitments reduce the number of new grants an IC can fund in a given fiscal year, lowering paylines and overall success rates (contributing to declines from ~21% to ~13% over recent years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that institutional budgeting choices and multi-year award obligations materially affect immediate funding prospects; submission and career strategies should account for reduced new-award capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant-chase / cumulative-submission strategy metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Cumulative probability calculations demonstrate that with lower success rates investigators must submit many more proposals to reach a desired cumulative probability of award (e.g., needing five more R01 proposals in FY2025 to reach the same 80% probability as in FY2023).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIs should use cumulative probability modeling to inform how many proposals they may need to submit to reach career or lab-level funding goals, balanced against time cost of proposal writing.
